newsitem.title: USA: Hughes, Raytheon decline comment on merger rumors.
newsitem.headline: Hughes, Raytheon decline comment on merger rumors.

text.p: Hughes Electronics Corp and Raytheon Co declined to comment Wednesday on rumors of a possible merger between the two companies.
A spokeswoman for Hughes, which is owned by General Motors Corp, said the company does not comment on speculation and a representative with Raytheon also declined comment.
A spokeswoman for GM also declined comment.
Shares of Hughes, the defense, automotive parts and electronics arm of General Motors, jumped 3-5/8 to 53-3/8. Raytheon was up 2-1/2 to 52-3/8 and GM was up 2-1/8 to 56-3/4.

Analysts expect both Hughes and Raytheon to be active in the coming year in the consolidation of the defense industry, although a merger of the two companies might produce difficult hurdles despite its obvious synergies.
"The concept that the two companies might want to get together is certainly not a new one," said Wolfgang Demisch, analyst at BT Securities.

"They have in the past been in talks; it's an on again, off again romance," said Joh Kutler of Quarterdeck Investment partners. "This rumor has been on and off for about a year ... it's one of the best fits in the industry."
A merger of the two companies would create the preeminent force in the tactical missiles market and make it a leading player in the radar market, something analysts say may cause anti-trust issues.
Demisch said the two firms are working together on a number of contracts so "the idea that they might work together more extensively is not that far fetched."

Demisch said obstacles to a possible merger would be how to treat General Motors ownership of Hughes for tax purposes and how to deal with certain assets, such as DirecTV, which may be better off as independent companies.
He also said the management style of the two firms may cause problems.
"There is a large number of individual issues that would need detailed attention, it would be a plausible transaction, but it would be a very demanding one," he said.
Both Hughes and Raytheon have said in recent months that they would consider large mergers and acquisitions should the right opportunity present itself.
Auto analysts said positive comments from a conference call on GM's new labor contract also contributed to the jump in the automaker's stock.
GM's new three-year pact with the United Auto Workers union requires it to maintain employment for 95 percent of its current hourly workers.

But during a briefing with investors on Wednesday, GM officials said the agreement gives it the flexibility to dramatically cut workers at troubled parts operations to keep the facilities competitive.
"People were favorably impressed. The loopholes in the 95 percent rule are bigger than everybody thought," said J.P. Morgan analyst David Bradley.

He said it is "a reasonable assumption" that the 12 troubled Delphi plants will be excluded from the job guarantee. GM has pledged to work with the union to make the plants more efficient, but if those efforts fail, it will be free to close or sell the plants.
Participating in the call were GM Chief Financial Officer Michael Losh and Gerry Knechtel, the company's lead negotiator for the talks.
